title: Boolean Masks & Set Logic
blurb: Comparisons produce arrays: combine masks logically and never loop over elements again.

cells.title: A boolean mask is an array you compute with
cells.body:
A comparison produces an array: g > 5 is a grid of True/False with the same shape as g. That mask is data — you can store it, combine it with &, |, ~, count it, and index with it: g[mask] returns the selected values as a 1-D array in reading order.

Counting is the key trick: on a boolean array, .sum() counts the True cells, so 'how many readings exceed the limit' is one comparison plus one sum. Selection and counting are the same mask used two ways — and because boolean indexing flattens in reading order, the selected values come out in a predictable, checkable order.

demo.code:
import numpy as np

g = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
m = g > 5
print(m)
print(g[m])         # selected values, reading order
print(m.sum())      # counting = summing the mask
print((g % 3 == 0).sum())

cells.title: NaN poisons comparisons — test for it explicitly
cells.body:
Every comparison with NaN is False: np.nan > 3 is False, and so is np.nan < 3 and even np.nan == np.nan. A float array with missing values therefore mis-classifies silently: NaN entries fall into every 'else' branch of a where-ladder and look like valid low readings.

The fix is a dedicated test: np.isnan(v) is the mask of missing entries, and it must be checked first in any priority ladder. Combine it with value conditions using & (with parentheses — operator precedence bites here), or let a nested np.where test it at the outermost level so the value ladder only ever sees clean numbers.

demo.code:
import numpy as np

v = np.array([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(v > 2)            # NaN compares False with everything
print(np.isnan(v))
print(np.where(np.isnan(v), -1, v))   # plug the hole first

exercise.title: Above the Limit
exercise.statement:
A compliance sweep must extract every reading that exceeds a legal limit, in the order the sensors were read (row by row, left to right).

Implement above_threshold(grid, t): return a 1-D int64 array of the values strictly greater than t, in reading order — one boolean mask, one indexing step. If nothing exceeds the limit, return an empty 1-D int64 array; that case is part of the contract, not an error.
constraints: grid is 2-D int64; t is a plain int
the result is 1-D int64 in row-major (reading) order
empty result (length 0) when no value exceeds t

examples.why: values 6 through 11 pass the limit; they come out in reading order
nothing exceeds 10, so the contract says: empty array

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def above_threshold(grid, t):
    """Return the values strictly above t, in reading order.

    grid is 2-D int64; the result is 1-D int64, empty if none pass.
    """
    pass
hints: One comparison gives you the mask; what does grid[mask] return, and in which order are the selected elements visited?
Boolean indexing flattens: grid[grid > t] is a 1-D array in row-major order regardless of the grid's shape, and it is empty when the mask is all False.
return grid[grid > t] — dtype int64 is inherited from the grid; for the no-match case numpy produces exactly the empty (0,) array the contract asks for.
exercise.reasoning: Boolean indexing is selection by predicate: grid > t computes a same-shape mask, and grid[mask] walks the array in reading order, keeping the elements whose mask cell is True — so the output order is row-major by construction, which is exactly what 'in the order the sensors were read' demands. The empty case needs no special code: numpy returns a length-0 array of the same dtype when the mask is all False, and that satisfies the contract (comparisons are dtype-, shape- and value-aware). The same mask also answers the counting question — (grid > t).sum() — so 'how many' and 'which ones' are one comparison apart.
exercise.solution:
import numpy as np

def above_threshold(grid, t):
    """Return the values strictly above t, in reading order."""
    return grid[grid > t]

exercise.title: IDs Seen Both Days
exercise.statement:
Yesterday's maintenance log lists the sensor ids that reported; today's log lists another batch (ids can repeat within a log). Operations asks: which ids were seen on both days?

Implement common_ids(a, b): return the ids present in both arrays as a 1-D int64 array, sorted ascending with each id appearing once. Build it with a membership mask (np.isin) and deduplicate with np.unique. If the two days share no id, return an empty array.
constraints: a and b are 1-D int64, each with at least 1 element; duplicates allowed inside each array
the result is sorted ascending, duplicate-free, 1-D int64; empty when there is no overlap

examples.why: 1 and 3 appear in both logs; each is reported once, ascending
heavy duplication on both sides still yields each common id once

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def common_ids(a, b):
    """Return the ids present in both arrays, sorted, deduplicated.

    a and b are 1-D int64; duplicates inside each array are allowed.
    """
    pass
hints: np.isin(a, b) returns a boolean mask with a's shape: True where the element occurs somewhere in b. What do you get when you index a with that mask, and what is still wrong with the result?
a[np.isin(a, b)] keeps a's surviving elements but preserves a's duplicates and a's order; np.unique sorts and deduplicates in one call, giving each common id once in ascending order.
return np.unique(a[np.isin(a, b)]) — for the no-overlap case this is the empty (0,) int64 array, which is the contract.
exercise.reasoning: Set questions on arrays decompose into mask, then tidy. The mask np.isin(a, b) answers membership per element of a against the whole of b in one vectorized pass; indexing a with it keeps the survivors — but survivors still carry a's duplicates and a's order, so the tidy step is np.unique, which sorts and deduplicates simultaneously. That two-step shape (predicate, then normalize) is the same one np.intersect1d implements internally — which is precisely what this composition computes. Note the ordering guarantee comes from the tidy step, not the mask: sorted output is a property you impose, and imposed properties are what make an expected array checkable.

exercise.title: NaN-Safe Classification
exercise.statement:
A float telemetry stream contains missing samples (NaN). Classify each sample into one of four codes, with missing checked first:

  • code 0 — missing: isnan(v)
  • code 1 — low: v < 10
  • code 2 — normal: 10 <= v < 25
  • code 3 — high: v >= 25

Implement classify_readings(v): return the code array as 1-D int64, same length as v, built with nested np.where where the outermost test is np.isnan. The order is not cosmetic: NaN compares False against every threshold, so if the value ladder ran first, every missing sample would silently masquerade as a low reading.
constraints: v is 1-D float64, length >= 1, may contain NaN
the result is 1-D int64, same length; code 0 iff the value is NaN
boundaries: 10.0 is code 2, 25.0 is code 3; the lowest band catches all v < 10 including negatives

examples.why: 8.0 is low, the NaN is missing (code 0, not low!), 12.0 normal, 30.0 high
exact edges: 10.0 opens the normal band, 25.0 opens the high band, 9.999 stays low

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def classify_readings(v):
    """Classify each sample; NaN (checked first) is code 0.

    Bands: 1 v<10; 2 10<=v<25; 3 v>=25. Returns int64 codes.
    """
    pass
hints: What is (np.nan >= 10) as a numpy expression — True, False, or an error? Decide what that implies for a ladder that never tests isnan.
Test isnan at the outermost level: np.where(np.isnan(v), 0, value_ladder). Inside the ladder every element is guaranteed non-NaN, so ordinary >= comparisons mean what they say.
code = np.where(np.isnan(v), 0, np.where(v >= 25, 3, np.where(v >= 10, 2, 1))); return code.astype(np.int64).
exercise.reasoning: NaN is the only value in numpy that is unequal to everything, including itself, so every threshold comparison involving it evaluates False. In a value-first ladder, that False sends each missing sample down the 'nothing matched' branch — the lowest band — and the misclassification is silent: the code array looks perfectly typed. Putting np.isnan at the outermost np.where flips the structure: the value ladder only ever sees elements guaranteed non-NaN, so its comparisons mean what they say. The general rule for any multi-condition mask: handle the poisoned values before the value conditions — whether the poison is NaN, ±inf, or sentinels like -999. Priority order is correctness, not style.
exercise.solution:
import numpy as np

def classify_readings(v):
    """Classify each sample; NaN (checked first) is code 0."""
    v = np.asarray(v)
    code = np.where(np.isnan(v), 0,
                    np.where(v >= 25, 3,
                             np.where(v >= 10, 2, 1)))
    return code.astype(np.int64)
